extraction.name: MATH
extraction.description: MATH is a dataset of 12,500 challenging competition mathematics problems, each with a full step-by-step solution. It is designed to measure the mathematical problem-solving ability of machine learning models.
extraction.creator: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Bums, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt
extraction.publisher: 35th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2021) Track on Datasets and Benchmarks
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The authors collected high school math competition problems from the Art of Problem Solving (AoPS) website, regenerated Khan Academy exercises using open-source code, and generated synthetic math problems using custom Mathematica scripts.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data consists of high school math competition problems with step-by-step solutions, Khan Academy exercises, and algorithmically generated problems from Mathematica. The text and equations are formatted in LaTeX, and figures are encoded in the Asymptote vector graphics language.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Achieving high accuracy on this dataset with machine learning models could enable students to cheat on their schoolwork, though it would also represent a profound intellectual and practical milestone.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is used to benchmark and measure the mathematical problem-solving ability of machine learning models. It is explicitly divided into training and testing splits for fine-tuning and evaluating models.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Upsampling and downsampling were used to balance the sizes of different data sources during pretraining.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Final answers were normalized using consistent formatting rules to enable exact match evaluation. This included simplifying fractions, standardizing fraction and coefficient encodings, and ordering variables alphabetically.

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: During pretraining, we upsample Khan Academy data by a factor of 5 and we downsample Mathematica by a factor of 2 to account for the large difference in dataset sizes.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: To assess models using exact match, we force the final boxed answers to follow consistent formatting rules. Specifically, probabilities are expressed as simplified fractions. Moreover, matrix entry fractions are encoded with x/y, while all other fractions are consistently encoded with the \frac{x}{y} command. Coefficients are encoded without a multiplication symbol (e.g. 5x not 5*x). Expressions with multiple variables are entered in alphabetical order; polynomials are expressed in decreasing degree order.
